title: Undertow and Inventory
premise: Xanthe Okonkwo, a professional letter-writer who composes postcards to an address that burned down years ago, has built his life on the careful inventory of everything unsaid. When Amara, the last fluent speaker of a dying language, asks him to become her final student and translate one untranslatable sentence before she dies, he must confront why his own mother's words were never passed down to him. As her health fails and his loyalty to her memory collides with the truth of what she actually did to survive, Xanthe learns that translation is not fidelity but choice—and in the end, he speaks the sentence aloud at her funeral, imperfectly, choosing truth over the comfort of silence.
about_author: Felix Ishikawa is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade translating testimony for people who could not speak for themselves. They live near a coastline that keeps erasing its own letters, and this is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Address That Burned
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We meet him writing postcards to 14 Marrow Lane, an address destroyed in a fire years ago, filing each unsent card into a meticulous inventory. His routine is interrupted by a hospital referral: a dying woman requesting a letter-writer. The beat is quiet unease—the machinery of his invisibility beginning to fail.

chapters.title: Amara Speaks in Three Tenses
chapters.summary: Xanthe visits Amara Osei in hospice; she refuses a letter and instead begins teaching him words from her language, which exists now only in her mouth. POV alternates between Xanthe and Amara's taped dictations. Emotional beat: reluctant fascination—he recognizes in her urgency something he fled from.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, structured as a literal inventory: items, debts, apologies never mailed. Flashback reveals his mother refused to teach him her own dying tongue, saying some things survive better untranslated. Beat: grief disguised as order-keeping.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Amara reveals there is one sentence—untranslatable, she claims—that she needs a second speaker to carry. She won't say what it means yet. Xanthe agrees to learn it without understanding it. Beat: a bargain struck in bad faith by both parties.

chapters.title: Lessons in a Dying Room
chapters.summary: Daily lessons begin. Amara teaches through objects: salt, thread, a chipped cup. Xanthe's POV with interludes of her grammar notes. He starts hearing his mother's cadences inside Amara's. Beat: the slow thaw of a man who planned to stay closed.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Xanthe investigates why 14 Marrow Lane burned, uncovering that his mother once lived there—with Amara. Their histories are braided together. Beat: vertigo; the past was never as sealed as his inventory implied.

chapters.title: A Letter Written Backwards
chapters.summary: Amara dictates a letter to someone named Efua, then makes Xanthe write it in reverse word order—a test, or a punishment. He keeps a copy against her instructions. Beat: first act of disloyalty, framed as devotion.

chapters.title: Efua
chapters.summary: Xanthe tracks down Efua, Amara's estranged daughter, who believes her mother abandoned her during a war neither will name. Efua's POV chapter. She knows fragments of the language too—fragments Amara doesn't know survived. Beat: the last speaker may not be the last.

chapters.title: Grammar of Survival
chapters.summary: Amara's dictations reveal how the language encodes survival: verbs that change depending on what you did to endure. Xanthe realizes the untranslatable sentence concerns what she did during the war. Beat: dread replacing tenderness.

chapters.title: The Postcard Returned
chapters.summary: One of Xanthe's postcards comes back stamped 'addressee unknown'—but with handwriting on the back: his mother's. Someone has been receiving them. Beat: uncanny rupture; the dead answering mail.

chapters.title: Two Students
chapters.summary: Xanthe secretly begins comparing his lessons with Efua's inherited fragments, assembling the language from two broken halves. Amara senses it and grows sharper, crueler in drills. Beat: triangulated suspicion and hunger.

chapters.title: What Amara Did
chapters.summary: Through a neighbor's account and a redacted archive page, Xanthe learns Amara informed on villagers—including possibly Xanthe's mother—to buy her children's safety. Beat: the price of survival made concrete and unforgivable.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Xanthe stops attending lessons. He writes furious postcards he finally intends to send. Amara's health collapses; the hospice calls. Beat: loyalty and truth pulling apart at full strength.

chapters.title: The Hospice Vigil
chapters.summary: Amara, half-lucid, teaches anyway, mistaking Xanthe for his mother at moments. He hears, for the first time, the actual sounds of the untranslatable sentence—without meaning attached. Beat: intimacy and horror fused.

chapters.title: Efua's Version
chapters.summary: Efua shares her fragment of the same sentence, learned as a lullaby—its meaning inverted: not confession but forgiveness. The two versions cannot both be true. Beat: revelation that translation itself decides guilt.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Marrow Lane
chapters.summary: Xanthe brings Amara's wheelchair to the ruins of 14 Marrow Lane. There she tells him the whole truth: she informed to save Efua, and his mother chose silence to protect her—and both women let the other believe the worst. Beat: climax of truth; grief reorganized.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Amara gives Xanthe the sentence's full meaning: it has no neutral form—it must be spoken either as accusation or absolution, and the speaker chooses. She asks him to choose after she dies. Beat: the weight of authorship passed on.

chapters.title: Last Light, Last Word
chapters.summary: Amara dies at dawn mid-lesson, the language leaving the world in her breath except for what lives in two students. Xanthe holds her hand through it. Beat: bereavement rendered in grammar—tenses failing him exactly when he needs them.

chapters.title: Choosing
chapters.summary: Xanthe's darkest hour: he drafts the funeral eulogy in English, safe and false, while the sentence waits in his notebook like a loaded thing. Efua demands he speak it her way; his inventory argues for silence. Beat: decision under pressure.

chapters.title: Eulogy
chapters.summary: At the funeral, Xanthe stands and speaks the sentence aloud—in Amara's language, in his own chosen inflection: absolution, but naming what she did. Half the mourners weep; Efua walks out. Beat: climax resolved into cost; truth spoken is never free.

chapters.title: Reconciliation of Accounts
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Xanthe and Efua begin compiling a dictionary from their combined fragments, arguing over every entry. He mails the final postcard—not to the burned address, but to Efua. Beat: mourning turning into practice, inheritance accepted.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Xanthe's POV at the shoreline where the language's last recorded words were first spoken. He teaches a stranger's child three words of it, imperfectly. The inventory book closes with one new entry: everything said. Beat: quiet resolution—survival as transmission, not preservation.
